entities.name: Activation Energy
entities.definition: The minimum energy that colliding reactant particles must possess for a reaction to occur, forming an activated complex. Activation energy governs the rate of a reaction through the exponential Arrhenius relationship with temperature.
examples: Hydrogen and oxygen mixed at room temperature react negligibly despite a favourable equilibrium because E_a is high.
A catalyst lowers activation energy, dramatically accelerating a reaction.
key_experiments: Measure a rate at several temperatures and extract E_a from an Arrhenius plot of ln k against 1/T.
common_misconceptions: All collisions lead to reaction (only collisions with energy above E_a are effective).
Raising temperature always changes the reaction mechanism (it increases the fraction of energetic collisions).
learning_objectives: Explain activation energy in terms of an energy barrier and activated complex.
Use the Arrhenius equation to relate rate constant to temperature.
Explain how catalysts lower activation energy.
real_world_applications: Designing catalysts for fuel cells and industrial synthesis.
Controlling reaction kinetics in food preservation and explosives.

provenance.source: IUPAC Compendium of Chemical Terminology

entities.name: Enthalpy
entities.definition: A thermodynamic quantity equal to the internal energy of a system plus the product of its pressure and volume, H = U + PV. The change in enthalpy, ΔH, measures the heat absorbed or released by a process at constant pressure.
examples: Burning methane releases heat, so the reaction has a negative enthalpy change (exothermic).
Melting ice absorbs heat from the surroundings, giving a positive enthalpy change (endothermic).
key_experiments: Dissolve a salt in water in a calorimeter and use the temperature change to measure ΔH of solution.
common_misconceptions: Exothermic always means hot to the touch and dangerous (exothermic is about the sign of heat flow, not harm).
ΔH and total heat are the same in every condition (ΔH equals heat only at constant pressure).
learning_objectives: Interpret enthalpy change as heat at constant pressure.
Distinguish exothermic from endothermic processes.
Apply Hess's law to calculate enthalpy changes.
real_world_applications: Calorimetry of fuels and foods to determine energy content.
Designing exothermic reactors and thermal energy storage.

provenance.source: Atkins' Physical Chemistry

historical.where: Lecture/publication in which the term 'enthalpy' was introduced
historical.context: Thermodynamic state function H = U + PV
historical.note: Kamerlingh Onnes coined the term 'enthalpy' in 1909. The underlying state-function concept (heat exchanged at constant pressure) was already present in earlier thermodynamics, including J. Willard Gibbs's work in the 1870s.

entities.name: Entropy
entities.definition: A thermodynamic quantity that measures the dispersal of energy or the number of microscopic arrangements (microstates) available to a system, expressed as a measure of disorder. The entropy of an isolated system tends to increase in spontaneous processes.
examples: Melting ice increases entropy as the solid lattice gives way to mobile molecules.
A gas expanding into a vacuum increases entropy because the molecules occupy more microstates.
key_experiments: Allow a gas to expand freely into an evacuated volume and reason about the increase in disorder.
common_misconceptions: Entropy is the same as chaos or mess (it is a measure of energy dispersal and available microstates).
Entropy can never decrease locally (entropy can decrease in a system if the surroundings compensate).
learning_objectives: Relate entropy to molecular disorder and the number of microstates.
Predict the sign of entropy change from states of matter and particle counts.
State the second law of thermodynamics in terms of entropy.
real_world_applications: Predicting the feasibility of processes via entropy and free energy.
Understanding the direction of heat flow and energy conservation in engines.

provenance.source: Atkins' Physical Chemistry

historical.note: Clausius coined the term 'entropy' in 1865, building on his formulation of the second law in the 1850s. He chose the name (from the Greek 'tropē', transformation) for its similarity to 'energy'.

timeline.event: Formulation of the second law of thermodynamics

entities.name: Equilibrium Constant
entities.definition: A dimensionless quantity that characterizes the position of a chemical equilibrium. For a reaction aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD it is the ratio of product concentrations raised to their stoichiometric coefficients to reactant concentrations raised to theirs, at a given temperature.
examples: For acetic acid ionization, K_a ≈ 1.8 × 10⁻⁵ at 25 °C indicates a weak acid.
A very large K for a formation reaction implies products dominate at equilibrium.
key_experiments: Measure equilibrium concentrations from a visible color change and compute K.
common_misconceptions: The equilibrium constant changes when concentrations change (K depends only on temperature for a given reaction).
Pure solids and liquids must always appear in K (their activity is taken as 1 and omitted).
learning_objectives: Write the equilibrium constant expression for a balanced reaction.
Interpret whether a large or small K favours products or reactants.
Distinguish K from the reaction quotient Q.
real_world_applications: Predicting the yield of industrial processes such as ammonia synthesis.
Estimating acid and base strengths via their equilibrium constants.

provenance.source: IUPAC Compendium of Chemical Terminology

entities.name: Gibbs Free Energy
entities.definition: A thermodynamic quantity, G = H − TS, that combines enthalpy and entropy to predict whether a process is spontaneous at constant temperature and pressure. A negative Gibbs free energy change indicates a spontaneous process.
examples: Ice melting above 0 °C is spontaneous despite being endothermic because TΔS outweighs ΔH.
A negative ΔG for rusting predicts that iron oxidizes spontaneously in air.
key_experiments: Mix solutions whose precipitate formation has known ΔG and observe spontaneity directly.
common_misconceptions: A negative ΔH alone guarantees spontaneity (entropy and temperature also matter via TΔS).
Spontaneous means fast (spontaneous only refers to thermodynamic favorability, not reaction speed).
learning_objectives: Relate Gibbs free energy to enthalpy, entropy, and temperature.
Predict spontaneity from the sign of ΔG.
Connect ΔG to the equilibrium constant and cell potential.
real_world_applications: Predicting corrosion, metabolic feasibility, and phase stability.
Designing batteries and assessing the viability of chemical synthesis.

provenance.source: Atkins' Physical Chemistry

historical.where: On the Equilibrium of Heterogeneous Substances (1876–1878), Transactions of the Connecticut Academy of Arts and Sciences
historical.context: Gibbs free energy and chemical thermodynamics
historical.note: Gibbs introduced the function combining enthalpy, entropy, and temperature (G = H − TS) in his memoir published across 1876–1878.

timeline.event: First part of 'On the Equilibrium of Heterogeneous Substances' published (series ran to 1878)

entities.name: Oxidation Number
entities.definition: A bookkeeping number assigned to an atom in a compound or ion that represents the charge the atom would have if all bonds to atoms of different electronegativity were ionic. Oxidation numbers track electron transfer in oxidation-reduction reactions.
examples: In H₂O the oxidation numbers are +1 for H and −2 for O.
In MnO₄⁻, manganese has oxidation number +7.
key_experiments: Use visible redox titrations, such as permanganate, to confirm electron-transfer stoichiometry.
common_misconceptions: Oxidation number is a real charge felt by the atom (it is a bookkeeping convention).
Atoms in a molecule must all have nonzero oxidation numbers (some atoms have oxidation number zero).
learning_objectives: Assign oxidation numbers by applying the standard rules.
Use oxidation numbers to identify oxidation and reduction.
Balance redox equations using changes in oxidation number.
real_world_applications: Naming inorganic compounds and balancing industrial redox processes.
Understanding oxidation states in corrosion and metallurgy.

provenance.source: IUPAC Compendium of Chemical Terminology

entities.name: Reaction Rate
entities.definition: The change in concentration of a reactant or product per unit time during a chemical reaction, usually expressed as the decrease in reactant concentration or increase in product concentration per second. Reaction rates depend on concentration, temperature, and the presence of a catalyst.
examples: The rusting of iron proceeds slowly, whereas a firework reaction is very fast.
Increasing reactant concentration raises the rate of a collision-controlled reaction.
key_experiments: Monitor a reaction by color change or gas volume over time and plot a rate curve.
common_misconceptions: The rate is constant throughout a reaction (rates generally slow as reactants are consumed).
Temperature has no effect on speed (each 10 °C increase typically roughly doubles the rate).
learning_objectives: Define and measure the rate of a reaction from concentration-versus-time data.
Explain how concentration and temperature affect rate via collision theory.
Contrast average rate, instantaneous rate, and initial rate.
real_world_applications: Controlling shelf-life and spoilage of foods and pharmaceuticals.
Designing industrial reactors and catalytic converters.

provenance.source: Atkins' Physical Chemistry

entities.name: Area
entities.definition: The measure of the size of a two-dimensional surface or region. Measured in square units. The amount of space enclosed within a boundary.
entities.equation: Rectangle: A = l × w  |  Triangle: A = ½ × b × h  |  Circle: A = πr²
examples: Room floor: 5m × 4m = 20 m²
Triangle base 10cm, height 6cm → area = 30 cm²
Field: 1 hectare = 10,000 m²
common_misconceptions: Area and perimeter are the same (perimeter is boundary length, area is enclosed space)
Larger perimeter always means larger area (a long thin rectangle can have large perimeter but small area)
Area units don't need to be squared (they must: cm², m², km²)
learning_objectives: Calculate area of rectangles, triangles, parallelograms, trapezoids, circles
Find area of composite shapes by decomposition
Convert between area units (1 m² = 10,000 cm²)
Solve real-world problems (flooring, painting, land area)
key_experiments: Grid paper: count squares to find area of irregular shapes

provenance.source: NCTM Principles and Standards / ICSE Mathematics Curriculum

entities.name: Combination
entities.definition: An unordered selection of items taken from a larger collection, where order does not matter. The number of ways to choose r items from n distinct items is C(n, r) = n! / (r! (n − r)!), often written as a binomial coefficient (n choose r).
examples: C(4, 2) = 6: from {a, b, c, d} there are six two-element subsets
Choosing 3 members of a committee from 5 people gives C(5, 3) = 10
C(5, 2) = C(5, 3) by symmetry C(n, r) = C(n, n − r)
The coefficients of (x + y)ⁿ are binomial coefficients C(n, r)
common_misconceptions: A combination counts the same as a permutation (a combination ignores order, giving fewer arrangements)
C(n, r) counts selections with repetition allowed (it assumes distinct items and no repetition)
learning_objectives: Distinguish combinations from permutations by whether order matters
Compute combinations with C(n, r) = n!/(r!(n − r)!)
Recognize binomial coefficients in expansion
Use combinations in probability counting
real_world_applications: Selecting committees, teams, or samples where order is irrelevant
Lottery and sampling probabilities built on unordered draws
key_experiments: Form all handshakes among a small group and count the unordered pairs to match C(n, 2)

provenance.source: NCTM Principles and Standards / Common Core State Standards for Mathematics

entities.name: Derivative
entities.definition: The instantaneous rate of change of a function with respect to its variable; the limit of the average rate of change as the interval shrinks to zero. Written f′(x) = lim_{h→0} (f(x+h) − f(x))/h, the derivative gives the slope of the tangent line to the graph at a point.
examples: If f(x) = x², then f′(x) = 2x
If f(x) = x³, then f′(x) = 3x²
The derivative of a constant function is 0
The derivative of f(x) = 3x + 5 is the constant 3 (its slope)
common_misconceptions: The derivative is the value of the function at a point (it measures change, not the function value)
A function must have a derivative everywhere (functions can fail to be differentiable at corners or breaks)
learning_objectives: Compute derivatives using the limit definition
Apply the power, product, quotient, and chain rules
Interpret the derivative as slope of a tangent and as instantaneous rate of change
Find extrema, tangents, and intervals of increase or decrease using derivatives
real_world_applications: Velocity and acceleration as derivatives of position with respect to time
Marginal cost and marginal revenue in economics as derivatives of cost and revenue functions
Optimization of area, volume, profit, and other quantities
key_experiments: Approximate instantaneous velocity by averaging over shrinking time intervals

provenance.source: NCTM Principles and Standards / Common Core State Standards for Mathematics

entities.name: Determinant
entities.definition: A scalar value computed from a square matrix that encodes geometric and algebraic properties of the matrix, such as whether its linear transformation is invertible. For a 2 × 2 matrix [[a, b], [c, d]] the determinant is ad − bc. A zero determinant means the matrix is singular.
examples: For a 3 × 3 matrix the determinant is found by cofactor expansion
The determinant of an identity matrix is 1
common_misconceptions: The determinant is defined for any rectangular matrix (it is defined only for square matrices)
A non-zero determinant and invertibility are unrelated (a non-zero determinant guarantees an inverse)
learning_objectives: Compute 2 × 2 determinants directly and larger ones by cofactor expansion
Use the determinant to decide invertibility of a matrix
Relate the absolute determinant to signed area in two dimensions
Solve systems using Cramer's rule where appropriate
real_world_applications: Testing whether a system of linear equations has a unique solution
Computing areas and volumes from coordinates of geometric shapes
key_experiments: Verify that det maps a pair of vectors to the signed area of their parallelogram

provenance.source: NCTM Principles and Standards / Common Core State Standards for Mathematics

entities.name: Integral
entities.definition: A quantity that accumulates a function over an interval: the definite integral ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx measures the signed area under the curve y = f(x) between a and b, while the indefinite integral is an antiderivative or a family of functions whose derivative is f. Integration reverses differentiation.
entities.equation: ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx  =  F(b) − F(a)  where  F′ = f
examples: ∫ 2x dx = x² + C
∫₀¹ x² dx = 1/3
∫ (cos x) dx = sin x + C
∫₀² 3 dx = 6 (area of a rectangle of base 2 and height 3)
common_misconceptions: The integral is only an area (it also accumulates any quantity being accumulated by the rate f)
The +C constant is unimportant (it is essential: antiderivatives differ by a constant)
learning_objectives: Interpreting the definite integral as accumulated change and signed area
Computing integrals of elementary functions using antiderivative rules
Relating the integrand f to its antiderivative F via the fundamental theorem
Using integrals to compute areas and volumes
real_world_applications: Computing distances, work, volume, and total change from rates of change
Accumulating probability over an interval from a density function
key_experiments: Approximate area under a curve with rectangles (Riemann sums), refining the partition

provenance.source: NCTM Principles and Standards / Common Core State Standards for Mathematics

entities.name: Mean (Arithmetic Average)
entities.definition: The sum of all values in a data set divided by the number of values. It represents the central tendency or "balance point" of the data.
examples: Daily temperatures over a week: sum of 7 values / 7
common_misconceptions: Mean is always one of the data values (it may not be)
Mean is unaffected by outliers (it is highly sensitive to extreme values)
Mean, median, and mode are the same (they differ for skewed distributions)
learning_objectives: Calculate mean for ungrouped and grouped data
Understand effect of outliers on mean
Compare mean with median and mode
Interpret mean in context
key_experiments: Balance point: find where a ruler balances with weights at data positions

provenance.source: NCTM Principles and Standards / ICSE Mathematics Curriculum

entities.name: Median
entities.definition: The middle value in an ordered data set. If there are two middle values, the median is their average. It divides the data into two equal halves and is robust against outliers.
common_misconceptions: Median is the same as mean (they differ when data is skewed)
Median requires the data to be numerical (ordinal data also works)
Median is affected by outliers (it is resistant to outliers)
learning_objectives: Find median for odd and even number of data points
Find median from frequency tables
Compare median vs mean for skewed distributions
Understand median as 50th percentile
key_experiments: Human median: line up by height, find middle person

provenance.source: NCTM Principles and Standards / ICSE Mathematics Curriculum

entities.name: Permutation
entities.definition: An ordered arrangement of a subset of items drawn from a larger collection, where order matters. The number of ways to arrange r items selected from n distinct items is P(n, r) = n! / (n − r)!; arranging all n items gives n! possibilities.
examples: P(3, 2) = 6: from {a, b, c} there are 3 × 2 ordered pairs
The letters of a 4-token word can be ordered in 4! = 24 ways
Choosing a president, vice-president, and treasurer from 5 people gives P(5, 3) = 60 ordered outcomes
P(n, 0) = 1 for any n (the empty arrangement)
common_misconceptions: Permutations and combinations are the same (permutations count ordered arrangements; combinations ignore order)
Factorials count arrangements only when all items are distinct (repeated items require dividing out repeats)
learning_objectives: Distinguish situations where order matters from those where it does not
Compute permutations with the formula P(n, r) = n!/(n − r)!
Use the multiplication principle to count ordered outcomes
Translate counting problems into permutation statements
real_world_applications: Ranking outcomes and scheduling where order determines meaning
Cryptographic and lock arrangements built on ordered selections
key_experiments: List systematically all two-letter arrangements of a small set to verify the formula by counting

provenance.source: NCTM Principles and Standards / Common Core State Standards for Mathematics

entities.name: Standard Deviation
entities.definition: A measure of dispersion that quantifies how spread out a data set is around its mean. It is the square root of the variance; for a set x₁, …, xₙ it equals sqrt((1/n) Σ (xᵢ − μ)²) where μ is the mean. A small standard deviation indicates values clustered near the mean, and a large one indicates wide spread.
examples: The set {5, 5, 5, 5, 5} has standard deviation 0
The set {2, 4, 6, 8, 10} has a small standard deviation
The set {1, 1, 10, 10} spreads far around its mean, giving a larger standard deviation
Standard deviation shares the units of the original data, unlike variance
common_misconceptions: Standard deviation and mean measure the same thing (the mean locates the centre; the standard deviation measures spread)
A larger range always means a larger standard deviation is needed in every set (range ignores order and clustering of values)
learning_objectives: Compute variance and standard deviation for a data set
Interpret standard deviation as a measure of spread around the mean
Compare data sets by their dispersion
Relate standard deviation to the normal-distribution model
real_world_applications: Assessing risk in finance through return volatility
Quality control, where the spread of measurements signals process variation
key_experiments: Generate two data sets with the same mean but different spreads and compare deviations

provenance.source: NCTM Principles and Standards / Common Core State Standards for Mathematics

historical.where: Statistical lectures and writings on the root-mean-square deviation
historical.note: Pearson introduced the standard deviation in the early 1890s as the root-mean-square deviation, building on Gauss's earlier method of least squares.

entities.name: Volume
entities.definition: The measure of the three-dimensional space occupied by an object or enclosed by a surface. Measured in cubic units. Capacity refers to how much a container can hold.
entities.unit: cubic metre (m³), cubic centimetre (cm³), litre (L = 1000 cm³)
entities.equation: Cuboid: V = l × w × h  |  Cylinder: V = πr²h  |  Sphere: V = ⁴/₃πr³
examples: Box: 2m × 3m × 4m = 24 m³
Water bottle: 500 mL = 500 cm³
Sphere radius 3cm → volume ≈ 113.1 cm³
common_misconceptions: Volume and capacity are the same (volume is space occupied, capacity is how much a container holds)
Doubling dimensions doubles volume (it multiplies volume by 8)
learning_objectives: Calculate volume of cuboids, cylinders, cones, spheres, pyramids
Convert between volume units (cm³, m³, L, mL)
Solve problems involving filling/emptying containers
Understand relationship between volume and capacity
key_experiments: Water displacement: find volume of irregular objects

provenance.source: NCTM Principles and Standards / ICSE Mathematics Curriculum

entities.name: Acceleration
entities.definition: The rate of change of velocity with respect to time; a vector quantity. Acceleration occurs whenever an object's velocity changes — whether in magnitude, direction, or both.
examples: A car speeding up from rest at a traffic light.
A ball slowing as it rolls uphill (negative acceleration).
key_experiments: Ticker-tape timer: the spacing of dots on a tape grows as velocity increases.
Rolling a ball down an inclined plane and measuring its increasing speed.
Motion sensor experiments recording velocity vs. time during acceleration.
common_misconceptions: Velocity and acceleration always point in the same direction (acceleration points in the direction of the change in velocity).
Acceleration always means speeding up (slowing down and changing direction are also acceleration).
If velocity is zero, acceleration must be zero (an object can have zero velocity and non-zero acceleration, e.g., at the top of a vertical throw).
If speed is constant, acceleration must be zero (changing direction at constant speed is still acceleration).
learning_objectives: Define acceleration as a vector quantity.
Calculate acceleration from change in velocity and time.
Distinguish between positive, negative, and zero acceleration.
Interpret acceleration from velocity-time graphs.
Explain situations where velocity and acceleration have different directions.

entities.name: Amplitude
entities.definition: The maximum displacement of a wave from its equilibrium (rest) position. Amplitude determines the energy carried by the wave — greater amplitude means greater energy.
real_world_applications: Loudness of a sound depends on its amplitude.
Earthquake amplitude sets the shaking damage; radio signal strength is an amplitude measure.
examples: A loud drumbeat produces a wave with large amplitude.
A gentle ripple on water has a small amplitude.
key_experiments: Oscilloscope: a louder sound shows larger wave amplitude at the same frequency.
common_misconceptions: Amplitude is the wavelength (amplitude is height; wavelength is distance between cycles).
Amplitude affects wave speed (wave speed depends on the medium, not amplitude).
learning_objectives: Define amplitude and identify it on a wave diagram.
Relate amplitude to wave energy.
Compare amplitudes of different waves.

entities.name: Capacitance
entities.definition: The ability of a system of conductors separated by an insulator to store electric charge, measured as the ratio of stored charge to the potential difference across the system. A capacitor is the device realizing this property.
examples: A parallel-plate capacitor stores charge proportional to the voltage across its plates.
In a camera flash, a capacitor discharges rapidly to deliver a bright pulse of light.
key_experiments: Charge a capacitor through a resistor and record the exponential growth of voltage.
common_misconceptions: Capacitance depends on the geometry and dielectric, not on the charge or voltage applied.
A capacitor in a DC circuit blocks steady current but stores and releases charge.
learning_objectives: Compute capacitance and stored charge for parallel-plate geometry.
Describe how a dielectric increases capacitance.
real_world_applications: Energy storage in battery-free memory and camera flashes.
Filtering and smoothing in power-supply circuits.

provenance.source: Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics

entities.name: Electric Current
entities.definition: The flow of electric charge through a conductor. Current is measured as the rate of flow of charge past a point in a circuit.
examples: A 2 A current flows through an electric iron; phone chargers draw fractions of an amp.
Household wiring carries alternating current.
key_experiments: Series circuit with an ammeter: the current is the same at every point in the loop.
common_misconceptions: Current is "used up" by components (current is the same throughout a series circuit).
Current flows from negative to positive (conventional current flows from positive to negative).
Higher voltage always means more current (depends on resistance too).
learning_objectives: Define current as the rate of flow of charge.
Calculate current from charge and time.
Measure current using an ammeter.
Distinguish between conventional current and electron flow.

entities.name: Density
entities.definition: The mass per unit volume of a substance. Density determines whether objects float or sink in fluids.
examples: Oil floats on water because it is less dense.
A full and an empty box have the same volume but different densities.
common_misconceptions: Heavy objects always sink (it depends on density, not just mass).
Density is the same as weight (density is mass/volume; weight is a force).
All solids are denser than all liquids (ice floats on water — ice is less dense).
learning_objectives: Define density as mass per unit volume.
Calculate density from mass and volume.
Explain floating and sinking in terms of density.
Measure density of regular and irregular objects.
real_world_applications: Ship design (steel ships float because they displace enough water).
Hot air balloons (less dense air rises).
key_experiments: Measuring density of a regular solid and an irregular solid using displacement.

entities.name: Displacement
entities.definition: The change in position of an object, measured as a straight-line vector from the initial position to the final position. Displacement has both magnitude and direction, making it a vector quantity.
examples: A hiker who ends 3 km north of the start after a 7 km walk has displacement 3 km north.
A runner going once around a 400 m track has displacement zero.
key_experiments: Map/playground walk: compare path distance with straight-line displacement using a trundle wheel and a bearing.
common_misconceptions: Displacement is always equal to distance (they differ when the path curves or reverses).
Displacement depends on the path taken (displacement depends only on start and end points).
learning_objectives: Define displacement as a vector quantity.
Calculate displacement from position data.
Distinguish displacement from distance in multi-segment motion.

entities.name: Distance
entities.definition: The total length of the path traveled between two positions, regardless of direction. Distance is a scalar quantity — it has magnitude but no direction.
examples: Reading the odometer of a car — total path length travelled.
The length of your round trip to school in kilometres.
key_experiments: Measure a curved path with a string, then compare with a straight ruler line for the same route.
common_misconceptions: Distance and displacement are always the same (they differ whenever the path is not a straight line).
Distance can be negative (distance is always non-negative).
learning_objectives: Define distance as a scalar quantity.
Distinguish between distance and displacement.
Calculate total distance traveled from a path description.

entities.name: Electric Charge
entities.definition: A fundamental property of matter that causes it to experience a force when placed in an electromagnetic field. Charge can be positive or negative; like charges repel, opposite charges attract.
examples: A balloon rubbed on hair attracts small paper pieces.
Lightning is a large flow of charge between cloud and ground.
key_experiments: Electrostatics: charge a balloon or rod by rubbing and detect it with a pith-ball or electroscope.
Charging a rod by friction and attracting small pieces of paper.
common_misconceptions: Charge is created by friction (charge is transferred, not created).
A charged object always attracts uncharged objects (a charged object can attract a neutral one through polarization).
Electrons are the only charge carriers (ions can also carry charge).
learning_objectives: Describe electric charge as a fundamental property.
Explain charging by friction, conduction, and induction.
State Coulomb's law and calculate electrostatic force.
Distinguish between conductors and insulators.

entities.name: Electric Field
entities.definition: The region of space surrounding a charge in which another charge experiences a force; quantified as the electric force per unit positive test charge at a point.
entities.equation: E = F/q (definition); E = k·Q/r² for a point charge Q
examples: The field around a point charge points radially outward for a positive charge and inward for a negative charge.
Field lines between two parallel oppositely charged plates are uniform and perpendicular to the plates.
key_experiments: Use a small test charge and a sensitive torsion balance to map the force and hence the field.
common_misconceptions: The electric field exists independently of any test charge placed in it; the test charge only measures it.
Field lines are not physical trajectories of moving charges; they represent force directions.
learning_objectives: Compute the electric field due to a point charge or a uniform field.
Sketch and interpret electric field lines for simple charge configurations.
real_world_applications: Capacitors store energy in their internal electric field.
Lightning rods and shielding use field concentration and cancellation.

provenance.source: Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics

entities.name: Energy
entities.definition: The capacity to do work or produce change. Energy exists in many forms and can be transferred between objects or converted from one form to another, but it is never created or destroyed.
examples: Stored chemical energy in a battery powers a bulb as electrical and light energy.
Kinetic energy of a moving bicycle is turned into heat by the brakes.
key_experiments: Pendulum: height at release swaps into speed at the bottom and back — evidence of energy transfer between forms.
common_misconceptions: Energy is a substance (energy is a property of systems, not a material).
Energy can be "used up" (energy is conserved; it only changes form).
Only moving objects have energy (stored energy — potential — exists without motion).
Heat and temperature are the same as energy (heat is energy transfer; temperature is a measure of average kinetic energy).
learning_objectives: Define energy as the capacity to do work.
Identify different forms of energy (kinetic, potential, thermal, electrical, etc.).
Explain energy transfers and conversions.
Apply the law of conservation of energy.
real_world_applications: Power generation (converting one form of energy to electrical).

entities.name: Frequency
entities.definition: The number of complete wave cycles passing a given point per unit time. Frequency determines the pitch of sound and the color of light.
real_world_applications: Radio and TV broadcast on assigned frequencies.
Mains electricity is 50 Hz; the pitch of a musical note is set by its frequency.
examples: Radio stations broadcast at different frequencies; mains electricity is 50 Hz.
A humming insect beats its wings faster than a bee — a higher frequency.
key_experiments: Tuning forks of different pitches viewed on a microphone + oscilloscope: higher pitch means higher frequency.
common_misconceptions: Higher frequency means larger waves (higher frequency means shorter wavelength).
Frequency depends on the medium (frequency is determined by the source; wavelength changes with medium).
learning_objectives: Define frequency and its unit (hertz).
Calculate frequency from period and vice versa.
Relate frequency to wave speed and wavelength.

entities.name: Gravitational Acceleration
entities.definition: The acceleration experienced by an object solely under the influence of Earth's gravity, near the Earth's surface. It is approximately constant for all objects, regardless of their mass.
examples: g ≈ 9.8 m/s² near Earth's surface — every freely falling object accelerates at this rate.
In vacuum a feather and a hammer have the same gravitational acceleration.
key_experiments: Measure g with a pendulum (T = 2π√(L/g)) or with free-fall timing gates.
common_misconceptions: g is the same everywhere in the universe (g varies with distance from a massive body).
g is a force (g is an acceleration; the force is weight = m·g).
Heavier objects have larger g (g is independent of the falling object's mass).
learning_objectives: State the approximate value of g near Earth's surface.
Distinguish between gravitational acceleration and gravitational force.
Apply g in free-fall and projectile motion calculations.
real_world_applications: Parachuting (terminal velocity involves balancing g with air resistance).

entities.name: Half-Life
entities.definition: The time required for half the nuclei in a radioactive sample to decay. It is a statistically defined constant for a given nuclide and independent of the sample size.
examples: Carbon-14 decays with a half-life of about 5730 years, used in dating organic remains.
A short-lived medical isotope loses half its activity in a matter of minutes.
key_experiments: Record the count rate of a radioactive source at successive times and show it halves each half-life.
common_misconceptions: Half-life is a statistical average, not a time by which every individual nucleus has decayed.
Heating, pressure, or chemical state do not change a nuclide's half-life.
learning_objectives: Apply the half-life relation to compute remaining nuclei or activity.
Use half-life to estimate the age of a sample via radiometric dating.
real_world_applications: Carbon-14 and potassium-argon dating in archaeology and geology.
Planning radiation therapy and managing radioactive waste decay.

provenance.source: Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics

entities.name: Heat
entities.definition: Energy transferred from one body to another due to a temperature difference. Heat is energy in transit — it is not stored in an object (the stored energy is internal energy).
entities.equation: Q = m·c·ΔT (specific heat) ; Q = m·L (latent heat)
examples: A flame transfers heat into a kettle of water; you warm your hands over a fire.
An iron rod conducts heat from its hot end toward the cool end.
key_experiments: Mix hot and cold water: measure the final temperature and relate heat gained by the cold water to heat lost by the hot water.
Measuring specific heat capacity of a metal using calorimetry.
Observing heat transfer between hot and cold water.
common_misconceptions: Heat and temperature are the same (heat is energy transfer; temperature is a measure of average kinetic energy).
Heat is stored in an object (heat is energy in transit; internal energy is stored).
Cold is a form of energy (cold is the absence of heat; heat flows from hot to cold).
learning_objectives: Define heat as energy transfer due to temperature difference.
Distinguish between heat and temperature.
Calculate heat transfer using specific heat capacity.
Explain why objects reach thermal equilibrium.
real_world_applications: Climate and weather (heat transfer in atmosphere).

entities.name: Heat Capacity
entities.definition: The amount of heat required to raise the temperature of an entire object by one unit of temperature. It depends on the object's size and material, unlike the intensive specific heat which is heat capacity per unit mass.
examples: A large metal engine block has a higher heat capacity than a small one, so it warms more slowly.
A full bottle of water resists temperature change longer than an empty one of similar surface area.
key_experiments: Supply a known quantity of heat to an object and measure the resulting temperature rise.
common_misconceptions: Heat capacity is an extensive property: it grows with the amount of material.
Heat capacity is not the same as specific heat, which is normalized per unit mass.
learning_objectives: Distinguish heat capacity from specific heat capacity.
Compute temperature change from supplied heat and heat capacity.
real_world_applications: Designing thermal reservoirs and engine cooling systems.
Choosing building materials with favourable thermal inertia.

provenance.source: Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics

entities.name: Impulse
entities.definition: The product of the average force acting on an object and the time interval over which it acts. Impulse equals the change in momentum of the object.
entities.unit: newton second (N·s) or kilogram metre per second (kg·m/s)
examples: Pulling your hands back while catching a fast ball lengthens the catch time and softens the force.
Crash padding in a car dashboard lengthens impact time and lowers peak force.
key_experiments: Egg-drop landing on foam versus hard floor: same impulse, longer time, smaller force.
common_misconceptions: Impulse is the same as force (impulse is force × time; it measures total momentum change).
A small force cannot produce significant impulse (over a long enough time, even small forces produce large impulse).
Impulse only occurs in collisions (any force acting over time produces impulse).
learning_objectives: Define impulse as force multiplied by time.
Relate impulse to change in momentum.
Explain how increasing collision time reduces average force.
Interpret force-time graphs to find impulse.
real_world_applications: Catching a ball (pulling hand back increases time, reduces force).
Pole vaulters landing on thick mats.

entities.name: Kinetic Energy
entities.definition: The energy possessed by an object due to its motion. The kinetic energy of an object depends on its mass and the square of its speed.
examples: A moving truck has far more kinetic energy than a bicycle at the same speed.
Wind turns turbine blades — the air's kinetic energy becomes electricity.
key_experiments: Ramp-and-block: objects released from higher ramps (more KE = ½mv²) push a block farther.
common_misconceptions: Kinetic energy is directly proportional to speed (it depends on speed squared — doubling speed quadruples kinetic energy).
Kinetic energy can be negative (kinetic energy is always non-negative).
Heavier objects always have more kinetic energy (at the same speed, yes; at different speeds, not necessarily).
learning_objectives: Define kinetic energy as energy of motion.
Calculate kinetic energy from mass and speed.
Explain why kinetic energy depends on speed squared.
Relate kinetic energy to work done on an object.
real_world_applications: Vehicle braking distance (doubles with the square of speed).
Sports (a faster ball has much more energy).
Wind turbines (kinetic energy of wind converted to electricity).

entities.name: Magnetic Flux
entities.definition: A measure of the total magnetic field passing through a given surface area, calculated as the product of magnetic field strength perpendicular to the surface and the surface area.
examples: Pushing a magnet into a coil links flux and induces current; more turns give more flux linkage.
Transformer cores concentrate the magnetic flux.
key_experiments: Move a magnet in and out of a coil connected to a galvanometer — deflection grows with speed and number of turns.
common_misconceptions: Magnetic flux and magnetic field strength are identical (flux accounts for total area and orientation).
A stationary coil in a constant magnetic field has changing flux (flux only changes when field, area, or angle changes).
learning_objectives: Define magnetic flux and calculate its value for a surface perpendicular to a uniform field.
State the SI unit of magnetic flux (weber).
Relate rate of change of magnetic flux to induced electromotive force.
real_world_applications: Electric power transformers and induction cooktops.
Magnetic field sensors and hall-effect probes.

provenance.source: IUPAP Symbols, Units, Nomenclature in Physics

entities.name: Magnetic Force
entities.definition: The force exerted by a magnetic field on a moving charge or on a current-carrying conductor. It is perpendicular to both the velocity of the charge and the magnetic field, so it changes the direction of motion but not the speed of a free charge.
entities.equation: F = q·v×B for a charge q moving at velocity v in field B
examples: A charged particle entering a uniform magnetic field at right angles moves in a circular path.
A current-carrying wire in a magnetic field experiences a deflecting force.
key_experiments: Pass a current through a wire suspended between magnet poles and observe perpendicular deflection.
common_misconceptions: A stationary charge feels no magnetic force; only moving charges or currents experience it.
The magnetic force does no work on a free charge because it is always perpendicular to velocity.
learning_objectives: Determine the direction of magnetic force using the right-hand rule.
Explain why a magnetic field alone cannot change a charge's kinetic energy.
real_world_applications: Particle accelerators and mass spectrometers steer beams with magnetic fields.
Electric motors convert magnetic force into rotational motion.

provenance.source: Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics

entities.name: Mass
entities.definition: A property of a body that quantifies its resistance to acceleration in Newtonian mechanics; an intrinsic property independent of location.
real_world_applications: Cooking measures ingredients by mass rather than volume.
Mass sets inertia and weight (W = mg), and drives spacecraft fuel budgets in orbit.
examples: A 1 kg bag of rice has the same mass on Earth and the Moon.
A beam balance compares amount of matter, independent of gravity.
key_experiments: Balance an unknown mass against standard masses with a beam balance.
common_misconceptions: Mass and weight are the same thing (weight is a force, W = m·g, and varies with gravity).

entities.name: Momentum
entities.definition: The product of a body's mass and velocity; a vector quantity that is conserved in closed systems. Momentum quantifies the "amount of motion" an object possesses.
examples: A heavy truck and a light car at the same speed — the truck has more momentum and is harder to stop.
A water jet from a hose carries small momentum but can wash soil away.
key_experiments: Collision carts: send one cart into an identical at-rest cart and observe the momentum exchange.
Colliding trolleys on a frictionless track to demonstrate momentum conservation.
common_misconceptions: Momentum and kinetic energy are the same kind of quantity (momentum is a vector measured in kg·m/s; kinetic energy is a scalar measured in joules).
A heavier object always has more momentum (momentum depends on both mass and velocity).
Momentum is conserved only in elastic collisions (it is conserved in all isolated systems).
learning_objectives: Define momentum as a vector quantity.
Calculate momentum from mass and velocity.
Explain why momentum is a useful quantity in collisions.
Apply the principle of conservation of momentum.
real_world_applications: Car crashes (crumple zones increase collision time, reducing force).

entities.name: Nuclear Binding Energy
entities.definition: The energy required to separate a nucleus into its individual nucleons, equivalent to the mass defect through the mass-energy relation. It reflects the energy released when a nucleus forms from its constituents.
entities.unit: joule (J) per nucleus; electronvolt (eV) per nucleon
entities.equation: E_b = Δm·c², where Δm is the mass defect
examples: Iron-56 has among the highest binding energy per nucleon, making it unusually stable.
Splitting heavy nuclei or fusing light nuclei releases energy as they move toward higher binding per nucleon.
key_experiments: Mass spectrometers measure nuclide masses; comparing them to constituent nucleons yields the mass defect.
common_misconceptions: Binding energy is not energy stored inside the nucleus as if it were fuel; it is energy that must be supplied to break it apart.
A bound nucleus has less mass, not more, than its separated constituents.
learning_objectives: Relate binding energy to mass defect via E = Δm·c².
Interpret the binding-energy-per-nucleon curve to explain fission and fusion energy release.
real_world_applications: Explaining why both nuclear fission and fusion release energy.
Assessing nuclide stability in reactor and weapon design.

provenance.source: Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics

entities.name: Potential Energy
entities.definition: The energy stored in an object due to its position, configuration, or condition. Gravitational potential energy depends on mass, gravitational acceleration, and height above a reference level.
examples: Water stored high in a dam holds gravitational potential energy.
A stretched rubber band stores elastic potential energy.
key_experiments: Pendulum/roller model: height at the top of a swing converts to speed at the bottom — potential to kinetic.
common_misconceptions: Potential energy is stored "in" the object alone (it is a property of the object-Earth system).
Potential energy can be negative (it depends on the reference level chosen).
Only height matters for gravitational PE (mass and g also matter equally).
learning_objectives: Define potential energy as stored energy due to position or configuration.
Calculate gravitational potential energy.
Explain the relationship between potential energy and work done against gravity.
Analyze energy conversions between kinetic and potential energy.
real_world_applications: Roller coasters (PE at the top converts to KE at the bottom).
Hydroelectric dams (water at height has PE).
Springs and elastic bands (elastic potential energy).

entities.name: Power
entities.definition: The rate at which work is done or energy is transferred. Power measures how quickly energy is converted from one form to another.
examples: A 60 W bulb transfers 60 J of energy every second.
A machine that does the same work in less time has more power.
key_experiments: Stair climb: measure your mass, the stair height and the time; compute power = mgh/t and compare walking vs running.
common_misconceptions: Power is the same as energy (energy is the total amount; power is the rate).
More powerful machines always do more work (work depends on power AND time).
Power is stored in batteries (energy is stored; power is the rate of delivery).
learning_objectives: Define power as work done per unit time.
Calculate power from work and time.
Convert between watts and kilowatts.
Interpret power ratings of electrical appliances.
real_world_applications: Electrical appliance ratings (light bulbs, heaters, motors).

entities.name: Pressure
entities.definition: The force applied per unit area on a surface. Pressure explains how forces are distributed over areas.
examples: A drawing pin concentrates force onto a tiny point.
Tyres and balloons hold air at pressure above the atmosphere.
common_misconceptions: Pressure and force are the same (force is total; pressure is force per unit area).
Pressure always acts downward (pressure acts equally in all directions in a fluid).
Larger area means more pressure (larger area means less pressure for the same force).
learning_objectives: Define pressure as force per unit area.
Calculate pressure from force and area.
Explain everyday examples of pressure (knives, shoes, hydraulic systems).
Distinguish between pressure, force, and area.
real_world_applications: Knives and cutting tools (small area = high pressure).
Snowshoes and camel feet (large area = low pressure).
key_experiments: Pressure in fluids increases with depth.

entities.name: Electrical Resistance
entities.definition: The opposition to the flow of electric current in a conductor. Resistance converts electrical energy to thermal energy.
examples: A thin wire resists more than a thick one; metal conducts far better than wood.
Heater elements are deliberately high-resistance so they heat up.
key_experiments: Vary the voltage across a fixed resistor and plot current against voltage — straight line at constant temperature.
common_misconceptions: Resistance is the same as voltage (resistance is opposition; voltage is potential difference).
Thicker wires always have less resistance (all else equal, yes — but length and material also matter).
Resistance is always undesirable (resistance enables heating, lighting, and control).
learning_objectives: Define resistance as opposition to current.
Calculate resistance from voltage and current.
Explain factors affecting resistance (material, length, cross-sectional area, temperature).
Use the resistance formula R = ρL/A.

entities.name: Specific Heat Capacity
entities.definition: The amount of heat energy required to raise the temperature of 1 kilogram of a substance by 1 kelvin (or 1 degree Celsius). Different substances have different specific heat capacities.
examples: Water heats and cools slowly — its high specific heat (~4200 J/kg·°C) moderates coastal climates.
Sand on a beach warms faster than the sea in sunshine.
key_experiments: Electric-heater method: measure electrical energy in (P·t), the temperature rise, and compute c = Q/(m·ΔT).
Calorimetry experiment to measure specific heat of a metal.
common_misconceptions: Specific heat is the same for all substances (it varies significantly — water has very high specific heat).
Higher specific heat means the object is hotter (specific heat is about how much energy is needed to change temperature, not the temperature itself).
Specific heat depends on mass (it is a property of the substance, independent of mass).
learning_objectives: Define specific heat capacity.
Calculate heat transfer using Q = mcΔT.
Explain why water is effective as a coolant.
Compare specific heats of different substances.
real_world_applications: Car radiators (water's high specific heat absorbs engine heat).
Cooking utensils (metals with low specific heat heat quickly).

entities.name: Speed
entities.definition: The rate at which an object covers distance — the total distance traveled divided by the total time taken. Speed is a scalar quantity.
examples: A car speedometer reads 60 km/h.
A marathon runner's average speed over the whole race.
key_experiments: Time a measured distance with a stopwatch and compute average speed.
Measuring the speed of a moving object using a stopwatch and ruler.
common_misconceptions: Speed and velocity are always the same (velocity includes direction; speed does not).
Speed is always constant (speed can change continuously).
Average speed is the average of speeds (it is total distance divided by total time).
learning_objectives: Calculate speed from distance and time.
Distinguish between speed and velocity.
Calculate average speed for multi-segment journeys.
Interpret speed from distance-time graphs.

entities.name: Temperature
entities.definition: A measure of the average kinetic energy of the particles in a substance. Temperature determines the direction of heat flow — heat flows from higher temperature to lower temperature.
examples: A clinical thermometer reads 37 °C body temperature; a room thermostat is set near 20 °C.
Melting ice stays at 0 °C even while it absorbs heat.
key_experiments: Calibrate a thermometer at the ice point and the steam point.
common_misconceptions: Temperature measures heat (temperature measures average kinetic energy; heat is energy transfer).
Temperature depends on the size of the object (temperature is independent of mass — a small hot object can have higher temperature than a large cold one).
Absolute zero is the temperature at which all motion stops (quantum mechanics prevents complete stop, but it is the theoretical minimum).
learning_objectives: Define temperature as a measure of average kinetic energy.
Convert between Celsius and Kelvin scales.
Explain why heat flows from hot to cold.
Use thermometers to measure temperature accurately.

entities.name: Thermal Energy
entities.definition: The total internal kinetic and potential energy of the particles in a substance, associated with their random motion and interactions. Thermal energy is related to temperature but distinct from it — it depends on mass, temperature, and the nature of the substance.
examples: Rubbing your hands converts mechanical energy into thermal energy.
Thermal energy from the Sun warms Earth's surface.
key_experiments: Compare how fast identical cans of hot water cool when wrapped in different insulators.
common_misconceptions: Thermal energy and temperature are the same (temperature is average kinetic energy per particle; thermal energy includes all particles).
Thermal energy is only in hot objects (all objects have thermal energy).
Thermal energy can be completely converted to work (second law limits conversion).
learning_objectives: Define thermal energy as the internal energy of a substance.
Distinguish between thermal energy, heat, and temperature.
Explain how thermal energy changes during heating and cooling.
Analyze thermal energy transfer in everyday situations.

entities.name: Time
entities.definition: The dimension that orders events from past through present to future, measured as the interval between two events. Time is a scalar quantity and one of the fundamental base quantities in physics.
key_experiments: Time repeated pendulum swings and average to measure the period with small error.
examples: Timing a 100 m sprint with a stopwatch.
The time for one complete pendulum swing is its period.
common_misconceptions: Time is the same as a clock reading (time is the dimension; clocks measure intervals of it).
Time passes at the same rate for all observers (at relativistic speeds, time dilation occurs).
learning_objectives: Define time as a fundamental physical quantity.
Measure time intervals using appropriate instruments.
Use time as the independent variable in motion analysis.

entities.name: Velocity
entities.definition: The rate of change of displacement with respect to time. Velocity is a vector quantity — it has both magnitude (speed) and direction.
examples: A plane flying 800 km/h due west — speed plus direction.
A car's velocity changes when it turns, even if speed is constant.
key_experiments: Motion sensor tracking a walk: velocity shows negative values when the walker reverses direction.
Motion sensor experiments plotting position vs. time to extract velocity.
common_misconceptions: Velocity is just speed with a direction (the vector nature has real mathematical consequences).
Higher speed always means higher velocity (if directions differ, they are different velocities).
Velocity must be constant to be defined (instantaneous velocity exists at every point).
learning_objectives: Define velocity as a vector quantity.
Calculate velocity from displacement and time.
Distinguish between average and instantaneous velocity.
Interpret velocity from position-time graphs (slope).

entities.name: Potential Difference (Voltage)
entities.definition: The work done per unit charge to move a charge between two points in an electric circuit. Voltage is the "push" that drives current through a circuit.
examples: A 9 V battery provides 9 V of potential difference across a circuit; household mains is roughly 230 V.
Voltage is the 'push' that drives charge around a circuit.
key_experiments: Measure the terminal voltage of a battery with a voltmeter at no load and under load.
common_misconceptions: Voltage and current are the same (voltage is potential difference; current is flow).
A battery creates current (a battery provides voltage; current depends on resistance).
Voltage is "used up" in a circuit (voltage drops across components, but energy is conserved).
learning_objectives: Define potential difference as work done per unit charge.
Calculate voltage from work and charge.
Measure voltage using a voltmeter.
Explain why voltage drives current.
real_world_applications: Electrical outlets (120V or 230V depending on country).

entities.name: Wave Speed
entities.definition: The speed at which a wave propagates through a medium. Wave speed depends on the properties of the medium, not on frequency or amplitude.
examples: Sound travels at about 343 m/s in air; light at 3×10⁸ m/s.
Deep-ocean tsunami waves can travel at hundreds of km/h.
key_experiments: Ripple tank: measure frequency and wavelength and verify v = f·λ.
common_misconceptions: Higher frequency waves always travel faster (in the same medium, all waves of the same type travel at the same speed).
Wave speed is infinite (all waves have finite speed — light travels at 3×10⁸ m/s in vacuum).
learning_objectives: Calculate wave speed from frequency and wavelength.
Explain why wave speed depends on the medium.
Compare wave speeds in different media.
real_world_applications: Thunder and lightning (light travels much faster than sound).

entities.name: Wavelength
entities.definition: The distance between two consecutive points in phase on a wave — for example, crest to crest or trough to trough. Wavelength determines the character of the wave (color of light, pitch of sound).
real_world_applications: The colour of light corresponds to its wavelength.
Antennas are sized to the wavelength they carry; X-ray wavelengths image bones.
examples: Red light has a longer wavelength than blue light.
Longer radio waves bend around hills more easily than short ones.
key_experiments: Ripple tank: measure the wavelength of periodic waves and change the wave generator frequency.
common_misconceptions: Wavelength is the height of a wave (height is amplitude; wavelength is distance between cycles).
All waves have the same wavelength (wavelength varies enormously — from kilometers to nanometers).
learning_objectives: Define wavelength and identify it on a wave diagram.
Relate wavelength to frequency and wave speed.
Compare wavelengths of different types of waves.

entities.name: Weight
entities.definition: The gravitational force exerted on an object by a massive body (typically Earth). Weight is a vector quantity acting toward the center of the gravitating body.
examples: A 1 kg mass weighs about 9.8 N on Earth but only about 1.6 N on the Moon.
A spring balance reads weight; a beam balance reads mass.
key_experiments: Measure weight with a spring balance and mass with a beam balance for the same object and compare number values.
common_misconceptions: Weight and mass are the same thing (mass is intrinsic; weight is a force that varies with gravity).
Weight is measured in kilograms (kilograms measure mass; newtons measure weight).
An object in free fall is weightless (weight still acts; apparent weight is zero).
learning_objectives: Distinguish between mass and weight.
Calculate weight from mass and gravitational acceleration.
Explain why weight changes with location (different planets, altitudes).
Distinguish between actual weight and apparent weight.
real_world_applications: Weighing scales (measure normal force, which approximates weight on level ground).
Engineering loads (structural design must account for weight).
Athletics (high jump records at high altitude where g is slightly less).

entities.name: Work
entities.definition: Energy transferred to or from an object via the application of force along a displacement. For a constant force, work equals the product of force and displacement in the direction of the force: W = F·d·cos(θ). Work is a scalar quantity measured in joules.
examples: Lifting a book from the floor to a shelf does positive work on the book.
Holding a heavy weight stationary does no work (no displacement).
Friction does negative work on a sliding block.
common_misconceptions: Work is done whenever a force is applied (work requires displacement in the force direction).
Holding an object stationary requires work (no displacement = no work, despite muscular effort).
Work is a vector quantity (work is scalar; force and displacement are vectors).
learning_objectives: Define work as energy transfer via force through displacement.
Calculate work done by constant and variable forces.
Distinguish positive, negative, and zero work.
Apply the work-energy theorem (W = ΔK).
real_world_applications: Vehicle engines (work done by combustion forces).
Electrical circuits (work done by electric fields on charges).
key_experiments: Measuring work done lifting masses with a force sensor and displacement sensor.
Investigating work done by friction on a sliding block.
Verifying the work-energy theorem with a dynamics cart on a track.

provenance.source: Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics, 12th Ed.

evidence.description: Heat flow Q analogous to charge flow I; Fourier vs Ohm
